title: Your Big Brain Might Be Thanks to Fruit
summary:
What if the reason you can read this right now is... fruit?

Here's the wow fact: about 4 million years ago, the brains of our early upright-walking ancestors weighed only around 300 grams. That's about the same as a medium apple. Today, the average human brain weighs about 1,500 grams — like 1.5 liters of water. That's five times bigger!

Scientists have long thought meat helped build our big brains. Around 2.5 million years ago, our ancestors started eating more meat. But a new study says sugary foods played a huge, forgotten role too.

Think about it: to find ripe fruit, you have to remember where it grows and when it ripens. "You need to remember where it is in the forest," says Jennie Brand-Miller, a nutrition scientist at the University of Sydney. Remembering things takes brain power — and bigger brains help you remember better. It's a loop!

Researchers studied data from chimps, humans, and three early ancestor species. They found our earliest chimp-like ancestors were mostly vegetarians, and fruit gave them more than two-thirds of their food energy.

They even gave the finding a fun nickname: SWEET — "sugars were essential in evolution too."

So meat and sugar aren't rivals. "I see them as parallel stories, not one replacing the other," Brand-Miller says.

Next time you bite into a juicy peach, remember: your amazing brain might owe a thank-you note to fruit.
why_it_matters: The fruit on your plate did more than taste sweet — it helped build the very brain you are using to read this, so snacking on fruit is feeding a very old habit.

background_read: Fruit is packed with natural sugar, and sugar gives the body quick energy — that is one reason our bodies and our brains love it.
Humans and chimpanzees (the African apes that are our closest living relatives) share a common ancestor that lived millions of years ago.
Scientists work out how big ancient brains were by studying fossils — old bones and skulls dug out of the ground.
Article_Structure: WHO: A research team including Jennie Brand-Miller, a nutrition scientist at the University of Sydney.
WHAT: A new study says sugary fruit, not just meat, played a big part in making human brains grow five times bigger.
WHERE: The work looked at data from chimps, humans and three early ancestor species, and was based at the University of Sydney.
WHY: Remembering where and when fruit ripens takes brain power — so bigger brains could help our ancestors find more fruit, and more fruit could help brains grow.

perspectives.description: The study says fruit sugar was a forgotten hero, and that meat and fruit worked together instead of one beating the other.
Some scientists think meat gave our ancestors the extra energy that made bigger brains possible, and fruit alone may not explain such a big change.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral: both stories run side by side
perspectives.description: Researchers like Brand-Miller see the two ideas as parallel stories, so the real answer probably involves both meat and sugary foods.
